security_audit.summary: Static detections are false positives caused by Markdown code formatting, Firestore Rules interpolation syntax, and security-focused prose. No command execution, network access, reconnaissance, or credential exposure is present. One semantic issue remains: the guidance to prefer `read` can unintentionally grant both get and list access.

remediation.issue: The skill recommends `read` instead of `get` or `list`.
remediation.suggestion: Use `get` and `list` separately when they need different authorization checks. Use `read` only after confirming that both operations require the same access policy.

semantic_findings.title: Overbroad Read Permission Guidance
semantic_findings.description: The instruction to prefer `read` over `list` or `get` can overgrant access because Firestore `read` covers both single-document reads and queries. Rules should distinguish `get` and `list` when their authorization requirements differ.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The guidance explicitly prefers the broader Firestore read operation without limiting it to cases where get and list have identical authorization requirements.

content.value_statement: Firestore Rules can expose private data when access and validation logic are incomplete. This skill helps create structured rules with least-privilege access, schema checks, and security test scenarios.
actual_capabilities: Maps collection paths, queries, data models, and access patterns in a codebase.
Drafts Firestore Rules with default-deny access and authentication checks.
Adds field, type, size, ownership, and immutable-field validation.
Designs role-based access controls and separates public and private user data.
Reviews counter updates, state transitions, paths, and replay protections.
Provides an attack checklist for testing generated rules before release.
limitations: It cannot prove that generated rules are free of vulnerabilities.
It depends on accurate application schemas, queries, and authorization requirements.
It does not provision Firebase resources or replace production security review.
Rule syntax and emulator tests require Firebase tooling in the target environment.

use_cases.title: Build a new application policy
use_cases.description: Create a starting rules file for a new Firestore application with authenticated ownership and schema validation.

use_cases.title: Protect collaborative data
use_cases.description: Define safe editor, viewer, owner, and administrator permissions for shared documents.

use_cases.title: Harden an existing rules file
use_cases.description: Refactor existing rules and test for update bypasses, role escalation, data leakage, and unsafe counters.

prompt_templates.title: Start a rules file
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this project and create a prototype firestore.rules file. List your data model assumptions and require authentication by default.

prompt_templates.title: Add document ownership
prompt_templates.prompt: Create Firestore Rules for a posts collection. Authors can create, read, update, and delete only their own posts. Validate title, body, author ID, and timestamps.

prompt_templates.title: Model role-based access
prompt_templates.prompt: Design Firestore Rules for a workspace application with owners, editors, and viewers. Keep role fields immutable for non-owners and validate every update.

prompt_templates.title: Test complex business logic
prompt_templates.prompt: Refactor these Firestore Rules and perform the full attack checklist. Check counters, state transitions, collection queries, PII separation, and batch consistency.

output_examples.input: Create rules for private user profiles and public posts.
output: Assumed data model for profiles and posts.
Rules that limit profile access to the owner.
Rules that allow public post reads without exposing profile PII.
A list of assumptions and tests to run.

output_examples.input: Secure a likes counter on each post.
output: A counter-update policy that limits changed fields.
A consistency check for one like per user.
A replay and batch-operation test checklist.

best_practices: Provide real collection paths, field types, queries, and user roles before generating rules.
Test rules in the Firebase Emulator Suite with allowed and denied requests.
Review generated rules before deployment and repeat tests after each schema change.
anti_patterns: Do not use generated rules unchanged when application requirements are uncertain.
Do not store public profile data and private personal data in the same document.
Do not grant broad read or write access merely to resolve permission errors.

faq.question: What does this skill create?
faq.answer: It creates or refines a prototype Firestore Rules file and documents assumptions, validation, and test scenarios.

faq.question: Does it make Firestore Rules secure by itself?
faq.answer: No. You must review the rules against your application behavior and test them before production use.

faq.question: Can it support public data?
faq.answer: Yes. Describe which collections and fields are public. Keep private data in separate documents or collections.

faq.question: Does it validate existing application queries?
faq.answer: It can identify and account for query patterns found in the codebase, but you must test them with Firebase tooling.

faq.question: Can it implement roles?
faq.answer: Yes. It can draft ownership and role-based policies while protecting role fields from self-escalation.

faq.question: Does it deploy the rules?
faq.answer: It can prepare rules and recommend validation commands. You control deployment and must review the changes first.
